blocks.content: Lecture 1: Introduction to Software Engineering and Object-Oriented Fundamentals

content.title: Analyze: Your Software Engineering Experience
content.instructions: Reflect on a software project you've worked on. Identify one concrete example where the code worked correctly but was difficult to modify or reuse. What made it problematic? Write down the specific issue (tight coupling, unclear structure, hardcoded values, etc.).
content.purpose: Activate prior knowledge; diagnose gap between 'working code' and 'engineered systems'

slides.speakerNotes: Welcome students warmly. Launch the reflection activity immediately to activate prior experience and surface the central problem this course addresses: code that works isn't enough. After 2 minutes, ask 2-3 volunteers to share examples. Listen for themes like 'couldn't change X without breaking Y' or 'copy-pasted code everywhere.' Use their responses to preview that this course provides systematic principles (quality attributes, OO design) to prevent these problems. This diagnostic helps students see why engineering discipline matters beyond basic programming competence.

slides.title: Course Structure and Objectives

content.title: Apply: Map Your Prior Experience
content.instructions: Think of a programming project you've completed (any language). Classify it: Construction (does it work?), Architecture (is it well-structured?), or Engineering (is it maintainable long-term)? Discuss with a neighbor which pillar was strongest and which needs development.
content.purpose: Connect course structure to personal experience; diagnose learning needs

slides.speakerNotes: After presenting structure, launch the activity to make pillars concrete. Students often conflate 'working code' with 'engineered system.' Circulate and listen for misconceptions. Debrief by noting most student projects emphasize Construction, while industry demands all three pillars. This diagnostic helps students self-assess gaps and understand why the course balances theory with practice. Emphasize portfolio allows demonstrating growth across all pillars throughout the semester.

slides.title: The Software Engineering Challenge

items: Modern systems: millions of lines, decades of evolution
Systematic methods based on proven principles

content.prompt: Graph showing exponential growth curve of software complexity over time (1970-2025), with annotations marking major challenges: mainframes (1970s), personal computing (1980s), internet era (1990s), mobile/cloud (2010s), AI systems (2020s). Y-axis: Lines of Code (logarithmic scale), X-axis: Years

slides.speakerNotes: Share the Ariane 5 rocket failure story - a $500M disaster caused by software reusing code without proper engineering analysis. Contrast a simple student calculator (100 lines) with enterprise ERP systems (millions of lines, hundreds of developers, decades of maintenance). Emphasize that 'it compiles and runs' is not enough for industrial systems. Statistics: ~70% of software projects fail or are challenged due to lack of engineering discipline.

slides.title: Quality Attributes: The Foundation

items: Correctness: Does it do what it should?
Robustness: Does it handle the unexpected?
Extendibility: Can it adapt to change?
Reusability: Can we leverage it elsewhere?

content.title: Analyze & Classify
content.instructions: Consider an online banking system. For each scenario below, identify which quality attribute is violated: (1) Transfer moves $99 instead of $100. (2) System crashes when user enters text in amount field. (3) Adding cryptocurrency support requires rewriting transaction code. (4) Authentication logic can't be used in mobile app.
content.deliverable: Share your classification with a neighbor, then discuss one example as a class.

slides.speakerNotes: After presenting the four attributes, run the think-pair-share activity to move from understanding definitions to applying them in context. Give students 90 seconds individual thinking, 90 seconds pair discussion. Expected answers: (1) correctness, (2) robustness, (3) extendibility, (4) reusability. Use volunteer responses to highlight that real systems face all four challenges simultaneously. This bridges conceptual understanding to analytical recognition of quality issues in concrete scenarios, preparing students for deeper exploration in subsequent slides.

slides.title: Correctness: Doing the Right Thing

items: Verification through testing and formal methods

content.prompt: Venn diagram with two circles: 'Specification' and 'Implementation Behavior'. Show complete overlap labeled 'Correctness', partial overlap labeled 'Partial Correctness', and non-overlap labeled 'Incorrect'. Use clean, professional styling with blue and green colors.

slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize that correctness is binary - software either meets its specification or it doesn't. Give examples: banking transfer must move exact amount, compiler must generate semantically equivalent code, medical device must deliver precise dosage. Distinguish between specification (what) and implementation (how). Note that correctness assumes normal operating conditions - abnormal cases are handled by robustness. Mention that formal specifications enable mathematical verification.

slides.title: Robustness: Handling the Unexpected

items: Fail-safe design: maintain safety under failure

blocks.content: Examples: Web server handling malformed requests, text editor auto-saving on low memory, database maintaining consistency after power failure

slides.speakerNotes: Distinguish robustness from correctness: correctness handles specified cases, robustness handles unspecified/exceptional cases. Real-world example: a web server that crashes on malformed HTTP requests is not robust, even if it correctly handles valid requests. Discuss defensive programming: validate inputs, handle resource exhaustion, provide meaningful error messages. Mention fail-safe vs. fail-secure: medical devices should fail-safe (stop safely), security systems should fail-secure (deny access).

slides.title: Extendibility: Embracing Change

items: Ease of adapting to specification changes
Modular design and separation of concerns
Design for change from day one

content.prompt: Side-by-side comparison showing two system architectures. Left side (Good): modular boxes with one highlighted in red showing localized change, other modules unaffected. Right side (Poor): tangled web of dependencies with one change in red causing ripple effects (shown in orange) throughout system. Label: 'Well-designed vs. Poorly-designed System Response to Change'

slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize that requirements always change - new features, regulatory updates, business pivots. Example: e-commerce system adding cryptocurrency payment without restructuring entire checkout. Good design localizes changes: adding new payment method shouldn't require modifying inventory management. Mention the Open-Closed Principle preview: open for extension, closed for modification. Poor extendibility leads to maintenance nightmares and eventual system rewrites. Object-oriented mechanisms like inheritance and polymorphism support extendibility.

slides.title: Reusability: Leveraging Existing Solutions

items: Using software elements across multiple applications
Economic benefits: reduced time and cost

content.prompt: Pyramid diagram showing reusability spectrum. Base (widest): 'Widely Reusable Libraries' (e.g., data structures, math). Middle: 'Domain-Specific Frameworks' (e.g., web, games). Top (narrowest): 'Application-Specific Code'. Arrows showing decreasing reusability upward, increasing specialization upward.

slides.speakerNotes: Highlight economic impact: reusable components dramatically reduce development time. Example: standard library collections (List, Set, Map) used in millions of applications - imagine if every project reimplemented these! Discuss the reusability spectrum: highly general (math libraries) to domain-specific (authentication modules) to application-specific. Note the paradox: making something reusable requires more effort upfront (generalization, documentation, testing) but pays dividends across projects. Object-oriented features like inheritance and generics enable reusability.

slides.title: Quality Attributes: Trade-offs in Practice

blocks.content: Three systems with different priorities: (A) Medical device firmware — safety-critical, infrequent updates. (B) E-commerce platform — frequent feature additions, third-party integrations. (C) Scientific computation library — used across multiple research domains.

content.title: Think-Pair-Share (4 min)
content.instructions: For each system, rank the four quality attributes (Correctness, Robustness, Extendibility, Reusability) by priority. Identify one trade-off decision each system faces. Think individually (1 min), discuss with neighbor (2 min), share insights (1 min).
content.deliverable: Justify your ranking: which attribute matters most and why? What gets sacrificed?

items: Medical device: Correctness/Robustness > Extendibility (stability over flexibility)
No universal ranking — context drives priorities

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates students from understanding interactions to evaluating real trade-offs. After pair discussions, solicit 2-3 responses for each system. Highlight that medical devices prioritize correctness/robustness even at the cost of harder updates (regulatory constraints, safety). E-commerce needs extendibility for competitive features, accepting some technical debt. Libraries sacrifice optimization for generality. Emphasize that recognizing these trade-offs is a core engineering skill — no design satisfies all attributes equally. Preview that OO techniques help balance competing demands systematically.

slides.title: Why Object-Oriented Programming?

blocks.content: Scenario: Library management system tracking books, members, and loans. Two designs: (A) Procedural—separate data files (books.dat, members.dat) with functions process_loan(), calculate_fine(), update_inventory(). (B) Object-Oriented—classes BOOK, MEMBER, LOAN with encapsulated data and methods.

content.title: Design Evaluation (4 min)
content.instructions: Compare both designs against our four quality attributes. Which approach better supports correctness, robustness, extendibility, and reusability? Identify one specific advantage OO provides. Think individually (1 min), discuss with neighbor (2 min), share verdict (1 min).
content.deliverable: Justify your choice: which design would you recommend and why?

items: OO: Adding late fee policy modifies LOAN class only (extendibility)
Procedural: Changes ripple across multiple functions
OO: MEMBER class reusable in other university systems (reusability)

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity asks students to critically assess design paradigms rather than passively accepting OO superiority. After pair discussions, poll the room and probe reasoning. Highlight that procedural design scatters related logic (loan processing touches multiple files/functions), making changes risky. OO localizes changes: adding email notifications affects MEMBER class only. Emphasize encapsulation's role: BOOK ensures valid ISBN, LOAN enforces return dates—invariants protected by design. Connect back to Slide 9's trade-offs: OO systematically supports quality attributes through structural mechanisms, not just conventions.

slides.title: Classes: Blueprints for Objects

items: Class as a type in the type system
Abstract data type with hidden implementation

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing BANK_ACCOUNT class. Top section: class name 'BANK_ACCOUNT'. Middle section (attributes): '- balance: REAL', '- account_number: STRING'. Bottom section (methods): '+ deposit(amount: REAL)', '+ withdraw(amount: REAL)', '+ get_balance(): REAL'. Use standard UML notation with minus for private, plus for public.

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce class as fundamental OO concept: a blueprint or template. Analogy: architectural blueprint defines structure of houses, class defines structure of objects. Class contains attributes (data, state) and methods (operations, behavior). Example: BANK_ACCOUNT class defines what it means to be a bank account - every account has balance and account number, supports deposit and withdraw. Class is also a type: variables can be declared of class type. Emphasize that class is abstract - it's a definition, not a concrete entity (that's an object).

slides.title: Objects: Runtime Instances

content.prompt: Object diagram showing three BANK_ACCOUNT instances. Top: BANK_ACCOUNT class box. Below, three object boxes connected to class with dashed arrows: 'alice_account' (balance: 1000.0, account_number: 'A001'), 'bob_account' (balance: 2500.0, account_number: 'B002'), 'carol_account' (balance: 500.0, account_number: 'C003'). Label: 'Class and its Instances'

slides.speakerNotes: Distinguish class (abstract template) from object (concrete instance). Analogy: blueprint vs. actual houses built from it. Each object has identity (alice_account ≠ bob_account even if they have same balance), state (current values of all attributes), and behavior (responds to method calls). Objects are created at runtime, exist in memory, and eventually destroyed. Multiple objects can be created from same class, each with different state. Example: three bank accounts for Alice, Bob, Carol - all instances of BANK_ACCOUNT but with different balances and account numbers.

slides.title: Encapsulation: Information Hiding

content.prompt: Conceptual diagram of an object as a circle with thick boundary. Inside (private): 'balance: 1000.0', 'internal_state', 'implementation details'. Outside boundary (public interface): arrows pointing to 'deposit()', 'withdraw()', 'get_balance()'. External clients shown as small boxes outside, accessing only through public interface. Label: 'Encapsulation Boundary'

slides.speakerNotes: Encapsulation is crucial for quality: it's the mechanism that enables extendibility and reusability. Two aspects: (1) bundling data with operations that manipulate it, (2) hiding implementation details. Example: BANK_ACCOUNT balance is private - clients can't directly modify it, must use deposit/withdraw methods. This enforces invariants (balance never goes negative) and allows implementation changes (store balance in cents vs. dollars) without affecting clients. Analogy: car dashboard (public interface) vs. engine internals (private implementation). Encapsulation reduces coupling between components.

slides.title: Introduction to Eiffel

blocks.content: Eiffel: A Language for Quality Software

items: Designed specifically for software engineering principles
Strong support for Design by Contract
Clear, readable syntax emphasizing concepts over tricks
Advanced features: inheritance, genericity, multiple inheritance

content.title: Analyze: Language Choice Trade-offs
content.instructions: Consider these two scenarios: (1) Teaching software quality principles to MSc students, (2) Building a commercial web application. In pairs, analyze which language characteristics matter most for each scenario and justify whether Eiffel or a mainstream language (Java/Python) better serves each purpose. Focus on how language features support or hinder the four quality attributes.

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce Eiffel and address 'Why not Java/Python?' Answer: Eiffel was designed by Bertrand Meyer specifically to teach software engineering principles with clean syntax emphasizing concepts. Design by Contract is built-in. The activity asks students to analyze trade-offs between pedagogical clarity and industry adoption, connecting language features to quality attributes from earlier slides. This develops critical evaluation skills: recognizing that tool choice depends on context and priorities. Debrief by emphasizing concept transferability—principles learned in Eiffel apply everywhere, like learning music theory on piano helps with any instrument.

slides.title: Eiffel Class Structure

content.code:
class
    POINT

create
    make

feature {NONE} -- Initialization

    make (a_x, a_y: REAL)
        do
            x := a_x
            y := a_y
        end

feature -- Access

    x: REAL
    y: REAL

feature -- Measurement

    distance_to (other: POINT): REAL
        do
            Result := sqrt((x - other.x)^2 + (y - other.y)^2)
        end

end

content.title: Apply: Extend the Class
content.instructions: Working individually, sketch how you would add a 'translate' feature that moves the point by dx and dy amounts. What feature clause should it go in? What parameters does it need? Does it violate encapsulation if it directly modifies x and y? Compare your solution with a neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: First walk through syntax: class declaration, create clause for constructors, feature clauses grouping related operations, attributes (x, y), methods (distance_to), Result for returns, := for assignment. Emphasize feature {NONE} means private initialization. Then launch activity: students apply the pattern by extending the class. This moves from passive observation to active construction. During debrief, highlight that translate can modify x and y because it's inside the class—encapsulation allows internal modification while controlling external access. Collect 2-3 solutions to show variation in approach.

slides.title: Eiffel Example: BANK_ACCOUNT

content.code:
class BANK_ACCOUNT
create make
feature {NONE} -- Initialization
    make (a_account_number: STRING)
        do
            account_number := a_account_number
            balance := 0.0
        end
feature {NONE} -- Implementation
    balance: REAL  -- Private
feature -- Access
    account_number: STRING
    get_balance: REAL
        do Result := balance end
feature -- Operations
    deposit (amount: REAL)
        require amount > 0
        do balance := balance + amount end
    withdraw (amount: REAL)
        require
            amount > 0
            amount <= balance
        do balance := balance - amount end
end

content.title: Analyze & Extend: Overdraft Protection
content.instructions: 1) Analyze: Why is balance private while account_number is public? What quality attributes does this support? 2) Apply: Sketch how to add overdraft_limit feature and modify withdraw to allow overdrafts up to the limit. Which feature clause? What precondition changes? 3) Share one design decision with a neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: Walk through encapsulation: balance is feature {NONE} (private), enforcing information hiding. Public interface: get_balance (query), deposit/withdraw (commands). Highlight require clauses as Design by Contract preview—preconditions enforce correctness. Launch activity: students first analyze design rationale (why this encapsulation?), then apply by extending functionality. This combines analytical thinking with practical application. During debrief, emphasize that overdraft_limit should be private, withdraw precondition becomes 'amount <= balance + overdraft_limit', supporting extendibility without breaking encapsulation. Collect solutions showing different approaches to initialization and validation.

slides.title: Course Roadmap

content.prompt: Course dependency graph showing progression of topics. Foundation layer: 'Classes & Objects', 'Encapsulation'. Construction layer (arrows from foundation): 'Inheritance', 'Polymorphism', 'Genericity'. Architecture layer (arrows from construction): 'Design Patterns', 'Large-Scale Structure'. Engineering layer (arrows from all): 'Agile Methods', 'Requirements', 'Quality Processes'. Use different colors for each layer, arrows showing dependencies.

slides.speakerNotes: Show how the course builds progressively. Today's fundamentals (classes, objects, encapsulation) are the foundation. Next: inheritance extends classes, polymorphism enables flexibility, genericity provides type-safe reuse. Then: design patterns as reusable architectural solutions (Strategy, Observer, etc.). Finally: engineering processes that tie it all together (Agile, Scrum, requirements engineering). Each topic builds on previous ones - you can't understand polymorphism without inheritance, can't appreciate design patterns without polymorphism. Emphasize the integration of theory and practice through tutorials and portfolio assignments.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

items: Four quality attributes: correctness, robustness, extendibility, reusability
Object-oriented programming supports quality through encapsulation
Classes are templates, objects are instances
Eiffel provides clear notation for learning OO concepts

blocks.content: Action items: Install Eiffel environment, read Touch of Class chapters 1-3, complete first tutorial exercise

slides.speakerNotes: Recap the main points: (1) Software engineering is essential for industrial systems - ad-hoc approaches fail. (2) Quality attributes are the foundation - correctness, robustness, extendibility, reusability. (3) Object-oriented programming provides mechanisms to achieve quality. (4) Classes and objects are fundamental concepts, with encapsulation as key principle. (5) Eiffel notation will be our vehicle for learning. Remind students of action items: install Eiffel, read assigned chapters, attend tutorials. Preview next lecture: inheritance (extending classes) and polymorphism (flexibility through type relationships). Encourage questions and office hour visits.

content.title: Analyze & Diagnose: From Failure to Principle
content.instructions: Read: Ariane 5 reused Ariane 4 altitude code. The new rocket's faster acceleration caused integer overflow, triggering self-destruct 37 seconds after launch. Which quality attribute(s) were violated? What engineering practice would have prevented this? Discuss with a neighbor, then propose one specific verification step the team should have performed.
content.purpose: Apply quality attributes to analyze real failure; connect abstract principles to concrete engineering practices

slides.speakerNotes: Present the Ariane 5 case as a concrete failure illustrating why systematic engineering matters. Launch the activity to move students from passively hearing the story to actively diagnosing it using quality concepts. Expected answers: robustness violated (didn't handle unexpected input range), extendibility violated (reuse without adaptation). Prevention: specification analysis, range testing, contracts. Debrief by collecting proposed verification steps, highlighting that engineering discipline means validating assumptions during reuse. This raises cognitive demand to analyze (diagnose root cause) and apply (map failure to quality framework), preparing students for the detailed quality attributes in Slide 4.

items: Correctness: Does it do what it should?
Robustness: Does it handle the unexpected?
Extendibility: Can it adapt to change?
Reusability: Can we leverage it elsewhere?

content.title: Diagnose, Classify & Propose Solutions
content.instructions: Online banking system scenarios: (1) Transfer moves $99 instead of $100. (2) System crashes on text in amount field. (3) Adding crypto requires rewriting transaction code. (4) Authentication can't be reused in mobile app. First, classify which quality attribute each violates. Then, propose one concrete design decision or practice that would prevent scenario (3). Share your solution with a neighbor and refine it together.
content.deliverable: Classification + one specific prevention strategy for extendibility failure

slides.speakerNotes: After introducing the four attributes, launch the activity. Give 90 seconds for individual classification and solution proposal, then 90 seconds pair discussion to refine prevention strategies, finally 60 seconds class debrief. Expected classifications: (1) correctness, (2) robustness, (3) extendibility, (4) reusability. For scenario 3, look for answers like 'use abstract payment interface' or 'separate transaction logic from payment method.' This elevates from pure classification to proposing preventive design decisions, bridging analysis to evaluation/creation. Highlight that quality attributes guide concrete architectural choices, preparing students for deeper attribute exploration in subsequent slides.

slides.title: Correctness: Doing the Right Thing

content.title: Identify Correctness Violations
content.instructions: Analyze this code snippet: A sort_list function specification states 'Sort integers in ascending order.' Implementation uses bubble sort but has condition: if (list[i] > list[i+1]) swap(). Which input reveals incorrectness? (A) [3,1,2] (B) [-5,3,-1] (C) [1,2,3] (D) All work correctly. Identify the answer and explain why it violates the specification.

slides.speakerNotes: Launch activity immediately after defining correctness. Answer is D—the code is actually correct for the specification. This challenges students to analyze specification-implementation alignment rather than just spotting bugs. After polling, reveal answer and emphasize that correctness requires complete specification coverage. If time permits, modify scenario: change spec to 'Sort all numbers' but keep integer-only implementation—now inputs with floats reveal incorrectness. Connect to next slide: correctness assumes valid inputs; invalid inputs relate to robustness.

slides.title: Robustness: Handling the Unexpected

items: Fail-safe design: maintain safety under failure

content.title: Diagnose Robustness Failures
content.instructions: Analyze these two implementations of withdraw(amount) for a bank account: (A) Subtracts amount from balance without checks. (B) Checks if amount > balance, displays 'Error: Insufficient funds' and prevents withdrawal. For each scenario, identify which implementation fails robustness and explain what abnormal condition is mishandled: (1) User enters -50 as amount (2) Database connection drops mid-withdrawal (3) User enters 'abc' as amount. Propose one improvement for the most critical gap.
content.deliverable: Identify failure cases and propose one robustness enhancement

slides.speakerNotes: Launch activity after defining robustness. Both implementations have robustness gaps: (A) fails all scenarios; (B) handles overdraft but not negative inputs, connection failures, or type errors. Critical gap is transaction consistency (scenario 2). Students should recognize robustness requires anticipating multiple abnormal conditions beyond obvious cases. After pairs discuss, poll for most critical gap and collect improvement proposals (e.g., transaction rollback, input validation). Connect to extendibility: robust error handling structures affect how easily we add new validations later.

slides.title: Extendibility: Embracing Change

items: Ease of adapting to specification changes
Modular design and separation of concerns
Design for change from day one

content.prompt: Side-by-side comparison showing two system architectures. Left side (Good): modular boxes with one highlighted in red showing localized change, other modules unaffected. Right side (Poor): tangled web of dependencies with one change in red causing ripple effects (shown in orange) throughout system. Label: 'Well-designed vs. Poorly-designed System Response to Change'

slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize that requirements always change - new features, regulatory updates, business pivots. Example: e-commerce system adding cryptocurrency payment without restructuring entire checkout. Good design localizes changes: adding new payment method shouldn't require modifying inventory management. Mention the Open-Closed Principle preview: open for extension, closed for modification. Poor extendibility leads to maintenance nightmares and eventual system rewrites. Object-oriented mechanisms like inheritance and polymorphism support extendibility.

slides.title: Reusability: Leveraging Existing Solutions

items: Using software elements across multiple applications
Economic benefits: reduced time and cost

content.prompt: Pyramid diagram showing reusability spectrum. Base (widest): 'Widely Reusable Libraries' (e.g., data structures, math). Middle: 'Domain-Specific Frameworks' (e.g., web, games). Top (narrowest): 'Application-Specific Code'. Arrows showing decreasing reusability upward, increasing specialization upward.

slides.speakerNotes: Highlight economic impact: reusable components dramatically reduce development time. Example: standard library collections (List, Set, Map) used in millions of applications - imagine if every project reimplemented these! Discuss the reusability spectrum: highly general (math libraries) to domain-specific (authentication modules) to application-specific. Note the paradox: making something reusable requires more effort upfront (generalization, documentation, testing) but pays dividends across projects. Object-oriented features like inheritance and generics enable reusability.

slides.title: Quality Attributes: Trade-offs in Practice

blocks.content: Three systems with different priorities: (A) Medical device firmware—safety-critical, infrequent updates. (B) E-commerce platform—frequent feature additions, third-party integrations. (C) Scientific computation library—used across multiple research domains.

content.title: Evaluate & Propose (5 min)
content.instructions: For each system, rank the four quality attributes by priority AND propose one concrete design decision that reflects your ranking. Example: 'Medical device prioritizes correctness, so I'd require formal verification of all updates before deployment.' Think individually (1.5 min), discuss with neighbor (2.5 min), share one proposal (1 min).
content.deliverable: Ranking + specific design decision for at least one system

items: Medical: Correctness/Robustness > Extendibility (formal methods, extensive testing, update restrictions)
E-commerce: Extendibility > Performance (plugin architecture, API versioning, feature flags)
Library: Reusability/Correctness > Specificity (generic interfaces, comprehensive test suites)
Trade-offs require explicit design choices—not just priorities

slides.speakerNotes: This enhanced activity pushes students from evaluation to creation by requiring concrete design proposals. After pair discussions, solicit 2-3 design decisions per system and probe how they operationalize priorities. Highlight examples: medical devices might use immutable data structures (correctness), e-commerce might adopt microservices (extendibility), libraries might use abstract base classes (reusability). Emphasize that recognizing trade-offs is insufficient—engineers must translate priorities into architectural choices. Preview that OO mechanisms (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism) provide systematic tools for implementing these decisions, which upcoming slides will explore.

slides.title: Why Object-Oriented Programming?

blocks.content: Scenario: Library management system tracking books, members, and loans. Two designs: (A) Procedural—separate data files (books.dat, members.dat) with functions process_loan(), calculate_fine(), update_inventory(). (B) Object-Oriented—classes BOOK, MEMBER, LOAN with encapsulated data and methods.

content.title: Design Evaluation (4 min)
content.instructions: Compare both designs against our four quality attributes. Which approach better supports correctness, robustness, extendibility, and reusability? Identify one specific advantage OO provides. Think individually (1 min), discuss with neighbor (2 min), share verdict (1 min).
content.deliverable: Justify your choice: which design would you recommend and why?

items: OO: Adding late fee policy modifies LOAN class only (extendibility)
Procedural: Changes ripple across multiple functions
OO: MEMBER class reusable in other university systems (reusability)

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity asks students to critically assess design paradigms rather than passively accepting OO superiority. After pair discussions, poll the room and probe reasoning. Highlight that procedural design scatters related logic (loan processing touches multiple files/functions), making changes risky. OO localizes changes: adding email notifications affects MEMBER class only. Emphasize encapsulation's role: BOOK ensures valid ISBN, LOAN enforces return dates—invariants protected by design. Connect back to Slide 9's trade-offs: OO systematically supports quality attributes through structural mechanisms, not just conventions.

slides.title: Classes: Blueprints for Objects

items: Class as a type in the type system
Abstract data type with hidden implementation

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing BANK_ACCOUNT class. Top section: class name 'BANK_ACCOUNT'. Middle section (attributes): '- balance: REAL', '- account_number: STRING'. Bottom section (methods): '+ deposit(amount: REAL)', '+ withdraw(amount: REAL)', '+ get_balance(): REAL'. Use standard UML notation with minus for private, plus for public.

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce class as fundamental OO concept: a blueprint or template. Analogy: architectural blueprint defines structure of houses, class defines structure of objects. Class contains attributes (data, state) and methods (operations, behavior). Example: BANK_ACCOUNT class defines what it means to be a bank account - every account has balance and account number, supports deposit and withdraw. Class is also a type: variables can be declared of class type. Emphasize that class is abstract - it's a definition, not a concrete entity (that's an object).

slides.title: Objects: Runtime Instances

content.prompt: Object diagram showing three BANK_ACCOUNT instances. Top: BANK_ACCOUNT class box. Below, three object boxes connected to class with dashed arrows: 'alice_account' (balance: 1000.0, account_number: 'A001'), 'bob_account' (balance: 2500.0, account_number: 'B002'), 'carol_account' (balance: 500.0, account_number: 'C003'). Label: 'Class and its Instances'

slides.speakerNotes: Distinguish class (abstract template) from object (concrete instance). Analogy: blueprint vs. actual houses built from it. Each object has identity (alice_account ≠ bob_account even if they have same balance), state (current values of all attributes), and behavior (responds to method calls). Objects are created at runtime, exist in memory, and eventually destroyed. Multiple objects can be created from same class, each with different state. Example: three bank accounts for Alice, Bob, Carol - all instances of BANK_ACCOUNT but with different balances and account numbers.

slides.title: Encapsulation: Information Hiding

content.prompt: Conceptual diagram of an object as a circle with thick boundary. Inside (private): 'balance: 1000.0', 'internal_state', 'implementation details'. Outside boundary (public interface): arrows pointing to 'deposit()', 'withdraw()', 'get_balance()'. External clients shown as small boxes outside, accessing only through public interface. Label: 'Encapsulation Boundary'

slides.speakerNotes: Encapsulation is crucial for quality: it's the mechanism that enables extendibility and reusability. Two aspects: (1) bundling data with operations that manipulate it, (2) hiding implementation details. Example: BANK_ACCOUNT balance is private - clients can't directly modify it, must use deposit/withdraw methods. This enforces invariants (balance never goes negative) and allows implementation changes (store balance in cents vs. dollars) without affecting clients. Analogy: car dashboard (public interface) vs. engine internals (private implementation). Encapsulation reduces coupling between components.

slides.title: Introduction to Eiffel

blocks.content: Eiffel: A Language for Quality Software

items: Designed specifically for software engineering principles
Strong support for Design by Contract
Clear, readable syntax emphasizing concepts over tricks
Advanced features: inheritance, genericity, multiple inheritance

content.title: Analyze: Language Choice Trade-offs
content.instructions: Consider these two scenarios: (1) Teaching software quality principles to MSc students, (2) Building a commercial web application. In pairs, analyze which language characteristics matter most for each scenario and justify whether Eiffel or a mainstream language (Java/Python) better serves each purpose. Focus on how language features support or hinder the four quality attributes.

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce Eiffel and address 'Why not Java/Python?' Answer: Eiffel was designed by Bertrand Meyer specifically to teach software engineering principles with clean syntax emphasizing concepts. Design by Contract is built-in. The activity asks students to analyze trade-offs between pedagogical clarity and industry adoption, connecting language features to quality attributes from earlier slides. This develops critical evaluation skills: recognizing that tool choice depends on context and priorities. Debrief by emphasizing concept transferability—principles learned in Eiffel apply everywhere, like learning music theory on piano helps with any instrument.

slides.title: Eiffel Class Structure

content.code:
class POINT
create make
feature {NONE} -- Initialization
    make (a_x, a_y: REAL)
        do
            x := a_x
            y := a_y
        end
feature -- Access
    x: REAL
    y: REAL
feature -- Measurement
    distance_to (other: POINT): REAL
        do
            Result := sqrt((x - other.x)^2 + (y - other.y)^2)
        end
end

content.title: Create: Design CIRCLE Class
content.instructions: Design a complete CIRCLE class with center (POINT), radius (REAL), and operations: make, area, contains (tests if a point is inside). Sketch the class structure showing: (1) Which features are public/private and why, (2) How your design supports correctness and encapsulation, (3) One precondition that prevents misuse. Share your design rationale with a neighbor, focusing on which quality attributes your decisions prioritize.

slides.speakerNotes: Walk through POINT syntax: class/create clauses, feature grouping, attributes versus methods, Result keyword, assignment operator. Emphasize feature {NONE} for private initialization. Launch activity: students synthesize a complete class design from scratch, integrating syntax patterns with quality principles from earlier slides. This elevates from applying a single pattern to creating a cohesive design. During debrief, collect designs on board showing different encapsulation choices (is radius public?), preconditions (radius > 0 in make), and how decisions reflect quality trade-offs. Highlight that internal use of POINT demonstrates composition.

slides.title: Eiffel Example: BANK_ACCOUNT

content.code:
class BANK_ACCOUNT
create make
feature {NONE} -- Initialization
    make (a_account_number: STRING)
        do
            account_number := a_account_number
            balance := 0.0
        end
feature {NONE} -- Implementation
    balance: REAL  -- Private
feature -- Access
    account_number: STRING
    get_balance: REAL
        do Result := balance end
feature -- Operations
    deposit (amount: REAL)
        require amount > 0
        do balance := balance + amount end
    withdraw (amount: REAL)
        require
            amount > 0
            amount <= balance
        do balance := balance - amount end
end

content.title: Analyze & Extend: Overdraft Protection
content.instructions: 1) Analyze: Why is balance private while account_number is public? What quality attributes does this support? 2) Apply: Sketch how to add overdraft_limit feature and modify withdraw to allow overdrafts up to the limit. Which feature clause? What precondition changes? 3) Share one design decision with a neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: Walk through encapsulation: balance is feature {NONE} (private), enforcing information hiding. Public interface: get_balance (query), deposit/withdraw (commands). Highlight require clauses as Design by Contract preview—preconditions enforce correctness. Launch activity: students first analyze design rationale (why this encapsulation?), then apply by extending functionality. This combines analytical thinking with practical application. During debrief, emphasize that overdraft_limit should be private, withdraw precondition becomes 'amount <= balance + overdraft_limit', supporting extendibility without breaking encapsulation. Collect solutions showing different approaches to initialization and validation.

slides.title: Course Roadmap: Your Learning Path

content.prompt: Course dependency graph showing progression of topics. Foundation layer: 'Classes & Objects', 'Encapsulation'. Construction layer (arrows from foundation): 'Inheritance', 'Polymorphism', 'Genericity'. Architecture layer (arrows from construction): 'Design Patterns', 'Large-Scale Structure'. Engineering layer (arrows from all): 'Agile Methods', 'Requirements', 'Quality Processes'. Use different colors for each layer, arrows showing dependencies.

content.title: Map Your Learning: Predict & Connect
content.instructions: Study the roadmap. Choose ONE upcoming topic (inheritance, polymorphism, design patterns, or agile methods). In 3 minutes: 1) Predict: Which quality attribute(s) will this topic primarily support? Why? 2) Connect: How might this topic build on encapsulation from today? Write 2-3 sentences, then share with a neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: Present the roadmap as a learning journey with clear dependencies. Launch activity to activate predictive thinking: students analyze how future topics connect to today's foundations and quality attributes. Common predictions: inheritance supports extendibility/reusability, polymorphism enables robustness through flexible interfaces, design patterns support reusability, agile supports correctness through iteration. During debrief, validate predictions and emphasize that each layer builds systematically—you can't master patterns without polymorphism, can't apply agile without understanding quality attributes. This metacognitive exercise helps students see the course as integrated rather than isolated topics.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

items: Four quality attributes: correctness, robustness, extendibility, reusability
Object-oriented programming supports quality through encapsulation
Classes are templates, objects are instances
Eiffel provides clear notation for learning OO concepts

(2) Quality attributes are the foundation - correctness, robustness, extendibility, reusability. (3) Object-oriented programming provides mechanisms to achieve quality. (4) Classes and objects are fundamental concepts, with encapsulation as key principle. (5) Eiffel notation will be our vehicle for learning. Remind students of action items: install Eiffel, read assigned chapters, attend tutorials. Preview next lecture: inheritance (extending classes) and polymorphism (flexibility through type relationships). Encourage questions and office hour visits.

slides.title: Introduction to Software Engineering and Object-Oriented Fundamentals

blocks.content: Lecture 1: Introduction to Software Engineering and Object-Oriented Fundamentals

content.title: Analyze: Your Software Engineering Experience
content.instructions: Reflect on a software project you've worked on. Identify one concrete example where the code worked correctly but was difficult to modify or reuse. What made it problematic? Write down the specific issue (tight coupling, unclear structure, hardcoded values, etc.).
content.purpose: Activate prior knowledge; diagnose gap between 'working code' and 'engineered systems'

slides.speakerNotes: Welcome students warmly. Launch the reflection activity immediately to activate prior experience and surface the central problem this course addresses: code that works isn't enough. After 2 minutes, ask 2-3 volunteers to share examples. Listen for themes like 'couldn't change X without breaking Y' or 'copy-pasted code everywhere.' Use their responses to preview that this course provides systematic principles (quality attributes, OO design) to prevent these problems. This diagnostic helps students see why engineering discipline matters beyond basic programming competence.

slides.title: Course Structure and Objectives

items: Three pillars: Construction (correctness), Architecture (structure), Engineering (long-term quality)
Assessment: 50% written exam + 50% portfolio demonstrating pillar integration
Eiffel notation → transferable OO principles for any language

content.title: Evaluate & Create: Diagnose and Redesign
content.instructions: Select a past project. (1) Evaluate it against all three pillars using a 1-5 scale for each. (2) Identify your weakest pillar. (3) Propose one concrete improvement that would strengthen that pillar (e.g., 'Add input validation for Construction' or 'Extract reusable modules for Architecture'). Share your proposal with a neighbor and explain why it addresses the gap.
content.purpose: Self-assess learning needs; create actionable improvement linked to course pillars

slides.speakerNotes: Present the three-pillar framework with brief examples: Construction ensures correctness through contracts, Architecture organizes complexity via modularity, Engineering sustains quality over decades through reusability and extendibility. Launch the activity to make pillars diagnostic and actionable. Circulate during pair discussions, listening for whether students grasp pillar distinctions. Debrief by collecting 2-3 proposed improvements and highlighting how the course provides systematic techniques for each. Emphasize that portfolio assessment rewards demonstrating growth across all pillars, not just producing working code. This activity raises cognitive demand to evaluate (self-assess against criteria) and create (propose targeted solution).

slides.title: The Software Engineering Challenge

items: Modern systems: millions of lines, decades of evolution
Ad-hoc approaches fail at scale → systematic methods required
Example: Ariane 5 ($500M loss from reused code without analysis)

content.title: Analyze & Diagnose: From Failure to Principle
content.instructions: Read: Ariane 5 reused Ariane 4 altitude code. The new rocket's faster acceleration caused integer overflow, triggering self-destruct 37 seconds after launch. Which quality attribute(s) were violated? What engineering practice would have prevented this? Discuss with a neighbor, then propose one specific verification step the team should have performed.
content.purpose: Apply quality attributes to analyze real failure; connect abstract principles to concrete engineering practices

slides.speakerNotes: Present the Ariane 5 case as a concrete failure illustrating why systematic engineering matters. Launch the activity to move students from passively hearing the story to actively diagnosing it using quality concepts. Expected answers: robustness violated (didn't handle unexpected input range), extendibility violated (reuse without adaptation). Prevention: specification analysis, range testing, contracts. Debrief by collecting proposed verification steps, highlighting that engineering discipline means validating assumptions during reuse. This raises cognitive demand to analyze (diagnose root cause) and apply (map failure to quality framework), preparing students for the detailed quality attributes in Slide 4.

slides.title: Quality Attributes: The Foundation

items: Correctness: Does it do what it should?
Robustness: Does it handle the unexpected?
Extendibility: Can it adapt to change?
Reusability: Can we leverage it elsewhere?

content.title: Diagnose, Classify & Propose Solutions
content.instructions: Online banking system scenarios: (1) Transfer moves $99 instead of $100. (2) System crashes on text in amount field. (3) Adding crypto requires rewriting transaction code. (4) Authentication can't be reused in mobile app. First, classify which quality attribute each violates. Then, propose one concrete design decision or practice that would prevent scenario (3). Share your solution with a neighbor and refine it together.
content.deliverable: Classification + one specific prevention strategy for extendibility failure

slides.speakerNotes: After introducing the four attributes, launch the activity. Give 90 seconds for individual classification and solution proposal, then 90 seconds pair discussion to refine prevention strategies, finally 60 seconds class debrief. Expected classifications: (1) correctness, (2) robustness, (3) extendibility, (4) reusability. For scenario 3, look for answers like 'use abstract payment interface' or 'separate transaction logic from payment method.' This elevates from pure classification to proposing preventive design decisions, bridging analysis to evaluation/creation. Highlight that quality attributes guide concrete architectural choices, preparing students for deeper attribute exploration in subsequent slides.

slides.title: Correctness: Doing the Right Thing

content.title: Identify Correctness Violations
content.instructions: Analyze this code snippet: A sort_list function specification states 'Sort integers in ascending order.' Implementation uses bubble sort but has condition: if (list[i] > list[i+1]) swap(). Which input reveals incorrectness? (A) [3,1,2] (B) [-5,3,-1] (C) [1,2,3] (D) All work correctly. Identify the answer and explain why it violates the specification.

slides.speakerNotes: Launch activity immediately after defining correctness. Answer is D—the code is actually correct for the specification. This challenges students to analyze specification-implementation alignment rather than just spotting bugs. After polling, reveal answer and emphasize that correctness requires complete specification coverage. If time permits, modify scenario: change spec to 'Sort all numbers' but keep integer-only implementation—now inputs with floats reveal incorrectness. Connect to next slide: correctness assumes valid inputs; invalid inputs relate to robustness.

slides.title: Robustness: Handling the Unexpected

items: Fail-safe design: maintain safety under failure

content.title: Diagnose Robustness Failures
content.instructions: Analyze these two implementations of withdraw(amount) for a bank account: (A) Subtracts amount from balance without checks. (B) Checks if amount > balance, displays 'Error: Insufficient funds' and prevents withdrawal. For each scenario, identify which implementation fails robustness and explain what abnormal condition is mishandled: (1) User enters -50 as amount (2) Database connection drops mid-withdrawal (3) User enters 'abc' as amount. Propose one improvement for the most critical gap.
content.deliverable: Identify failure cases and propose one robustness enhancement

slides.speakerNotes: Launch activity after defining robustness. Both implementations have robustness gaps: (A) fails all scenarios; (B) handles overdraft but not negative inputs, connection failures, or type errors. Critical gap is transaction consistency (scenario 2). Students should recognize robustness requires anticipating multiple abnormal conditions beyond obvious cases. After pairs discuss, poll for most critical gap and collect improvement proposals (e.g., transaction rollback, input validation). Connect to extendibility: robust error handling structures affect how easily we add new validations later.

slides.title: Extendibility: Embracing Change

items: Ease of adapting to specification changes
Modular design and separation of concerns
Design for change from day one

content.prompt: Side-by-side comparison showing two system architectures. Left side (Good): modular boxes with one highlighted in red showing localized change, other modules unaffected. Right side (Poor): tangled web of dependencies with one change in red causing ripple effects (shown in orange) throughout system. Label: 'Well-designed vs. Poorly-designed System Response to Change'

slides.speakerNotes: Emphasize that requirements always change - new features, regulatory updates, business pivots. Example: e-commerce system adding cryptocurrency payment without restructuring entire checkout. Good design localizes changes: adding new payment method shouldn't require modifying inventory management. Mention the Open-Closed Principle preview: open for extension, closed for modification. Poor extendibility leads to maintenance nightmares and eventual system rewrites. Object-oriented mechanisms like inheritance and polymorphism support extendibility.

slides.title: Reusability: Leveraging Existing Solutions

items: Using software elements across multiple applications
Economic benefits: reduced time and cost

content.prompt: Pyramid diagram showing reusability spectrum. Base (widest): 'Widely Reusable Libraries' (e.g., data structures, math). Middle: 'Domain-Specific Frameworks' (e.g., web, games). Top (narrowest): 'Application-Specific Code'. Arrows showing decreasing reusability upward, increasing specialization upward.

slides.speakerNotes: Highlight economic impact: reusable components dramatically reduce development time. Example: standard library collections (List, Set, Map) used in millions of applications - imagine if every project reimplemented these! Discuss the reusability spectrum: highly general (math libraries) to domain-specific (authentication modules) to application-specific. Note the paradox: making something reusable requires more effort upfront (generalization, documentation, testing) but pays dividends across projects. Object-oriented features like inheritance and generics enable reusability.

slides.title: Quality Attributes: Trade-offs in Practice

blocks.content: Three systems with different priorities: (A) Medical device firmware—safety-critical, infrequent updates. (B) E-commerce platform—frequent feature additions, third-party integrations. (C) Scientific computation library—used across multiple research domains.

content.title: Evaluate & Propose (5 min)
content.instructions: For each system, rank the four quality attributes by priority AND propose one concrete design decision that reflects your ranking. Example: 'Medical device prioritizes correctness, so I'd require formal verification of all updates before deployment.' Think individually (1.5 min), discuss with neighbor (2.5 min), share one proposal (1 min).
content.deliverable: Ranking + specific design decision for at least one system

items: Medical: Correctness/Robustness > Extendibility (formal methods, extensive testing, update restrictions)
E-commerce: Extendibility > Performance (plugin architecture, API versioning, feature flags)
Library: Reusability/Correctness > Specificity (generic interfaces, comprehensive test suites)
Trade-offs require explicit design choices—not just priorities

slides.speakerNotes: This enhanced activity pushes students from evaluation to creation by requiring concrete design proposals. After pair discussions, solicit 2-3 design decisions per system and probe how they operationalize priorities. Highlight examples: medical devices might use immutable data structures (correctness), e-commerce might adopt microservices (extendibility), libraries might use abstract base classes (reusability). Emphasize that recognizing trade-offs is insufficient—engineers must translate priorities into architectural choices. Preview that OO mechanisms (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism) provide systematic tools for implementing these decisions, which upcoming slides will explore.

slides.title: Why Object-Oriented Programming?

blocks.content: Scenario: Library management system tracking books, members, and loans. Two designs: (A) Procedural—separate data files (books.dat, members.dat) with functions process_loan(), calculate_fine(), update_inventory(). (B) Object-Oriented—classes BOOK, MEMBER, LOAN with encapsulated data and methods.

content.title: Design Evaluation (4 min)
content.instructions: Compare both designs against our four quality attributes. Which approach better supports correctness, robustness, extendibility, and reusability? Identify one specific advantage OO provides. Think individually (1 min), discuss with neighbor (2 min), share verdict (1 min).
content.deliverable: Justify your choice: which design would you recommend and why?

items: OO: Adding late fee policy modifies LOAN class only (extendibility)
Procedural: Changes ripple across multiple functions
OO: MEMBER class reusable in other university systems (reusability)

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity asks students to critically assess design paradigms rather than passively accepting OO superiority. After pair discussions, poll the room and probe reasoning. Highlight that procedural design scatters related logic (loan processing touches multiple files/functions), making changes risky. OO localizes changes: adding email notifications affects MEMBER class only. Emphasize encapsulation's role: BOOK ensures valid ISBN, LOAN enforces return dates—invariants protected by design. Connect back to Slide 9's trade-offs: OO systematically supports quality attributes through structural mechanisms, not just conventions.

slides.title: Classes: Blueprints for Objects

items: Class as a type in the type system
Abstract data type with hidden implementation

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing BANK_ACCOUNT class. Top section: class name 'BANK_ACCOUNT'. Middle section (attributes): '- balance: REAL', '- account_number: STRING'. Bottom section (methods): '+ deposit(amount: REAL)', '+ withdraw(amount: REAL)', '+ get_balance(): REAL'. Use standard UML notation with minus for private, plus for public.

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce class as fundamental OO concept: a blueprint or template. Analogy: architectural blueprint defines structure of houses, class defines structure of objects. Class contains attributes (data, state) and methods (operations, behavior). Example: BANK_ACCOUNT class defines what it means to be a bank account - every account has balance and account number, supports deposit and withdraw. Class is also a type: variables can be declared of class type. Emphasize that class is abstract - it's a definition, not a concrete entity (that's an object).

slides.title: Objects: Runtime Instances

content.prompt: Object diagram showing three BANK_ACCOUNT instances. Top: BANK_ACCOUNT class box. Below, three object boxes connected to class with dashed arrows: 'alice_account' (balance: 1000.0, account_number: 'A001'), 'bob_account' (balance: 2500.0, account_number: 'B002'), 'carol_account' (balance: 500.0, account_number: 'C003'). Label: 'Class and its Instances'

slides.speakerNotes: Distinguish class (abstract template) from object (concrete instance). Analogy: blueprint vs. actual houses built from it. Each object has identity (alice_account ≠ bob_account even if they have same balance), state (current values of all attributes), and behavior (responds to method calls). Objects are created at runtime, exist in memory, and eventually destroyed. Multiple objects can be created from same class, each with different state. Example: three bank accounts for Alice, Bob, Carol - all instances of BANK_ACCOUNT but with different balances and account numbers.

slides.title: Encapsulation: Information Hiding

content.prompt: Conceptual diagram of an object as a circle with thick boundary. Inside (private): 'balance: 1000.0', 'internal_state', 'implementation details'. Outside boundary (public interface): arrows pointing to 'deposit()', 'withdraw()', 'get_balance()'. External clients shown as small boxes outside, accessing only through public interface. Label: 'Encapsulation Boundary'

slides.speakerNotes: Encapsulation is crucial for quality: it's the mechanism that enables extendibility and reusability. Two aspects: (1) bundling data with operations that manipulate it, (2) hiding implementation details. Example: BANK_ACCOUNT balance is private - clients can't directly modify it, must use deposit/withdraw methods. This enforces invariants (balance never goes negative) and allows implementation changes (store balance in cents vs. dollars) without affecting clients. Analogy: car dashboard (public interface) vs. engine internals (private implementation). Encapsulation reduces coupling between components.

slides.title: Introduction to Eiffel

blocks.content: Eiffel: A Language for Quality Software

items: Designed specifically for software engineering principles
Strong support for Design by Contract
Clear, readable syntax emphasizing concepts over tricks
Advanced features: inheritance, genericity, multiple inheritance

content.title: Analyze: Language Choice Trade-offs
content.instructions: Consider these two scenarios: (1) Teaching software quality principles to MSc students, (2) Building a commercial web application. In pairs, analyze which language characteristics matter most for each scenario and justify whether Eiffel or a mainstream language (Java/Python) better serves each purpose. Focus on how language features support or hinder the four quality attributes.

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce Eiffel and address 'Why not Java/Python?' Answer: Eiffel was designed by Bertrand Meyer specifically to teach software engineering principles with clean syntax emphasizing concepts. Design by Contract is built-in. The activity asks students to analyze trade-offs between pedagogical clarity and industry adoption, connecting language features to quality attributes from earlier slides. This develops critical evaluation skills: recognizing that tool choice depends on context and priorities. Debrief by emphasizing concept transferability—principles learned in Eiffel apply everywhere, like learning music theory on piano helps with any instrument.

slides.title: Eiffel Class Structure

content.code:
class POINT
create make
feature {NONE} -- Initialization
    make (a_x, a_y: REAL)
        do
            x := a_x
            y := a_y
        end
feature -- Access
    x: REAL
    y: REAL
feature -- Measurement
    distance_to (other: POINT): REAL
        do
            Result := sqrt((x - other.x)^2 + (y - other.y)^2)
        end
end

content.title: Create: Design CIRCLE Class
content.instructions: Design a complete CIRCLE class with center (POINT), radius (REAL), and operations: make, area, contains (tests if a point is inside). Sketch the class structure showing: (1) Which features are public/private and why, (2) How your design supports correctness and encapsulation, (3) One precondition that prevents misuse. Share your design rationale with a neighbor, focusing on which quality attributes your decisions prioritize.

slides.speakerNotes: Walk through POINT syntax: class/create clauses, feature grouping, attributes versus methods, Result keyword, assignment operator. Emphasize feature {NONE} for private initialization. Launch activity: students synthesize a complete class design from scratch, integrating syntax patterns with quality principles from earlier slides. This elevates from applying a single pattern to creating a cohesive design. During debrief, collect designs on board showing different encapsulation choices (is radius public?), preconditions (radius > 0 in make), and how decisions reflect quality trade-offs. Highlight that internal use of POINT demonstrates composition.

slides.title: Eiffel Example: BANK_ACCOUNT

content.code:
class BANK_ACCOUNT
create make
feature {NONE} -- Initialization
    make (a_account_number: STRING)
        do
            account_number := a_account_number
            balance := 0.0
        end
feature {NONE} -- Implementation
    balance: REAL  -- Private
feature -- Access
    account_number: STRING
    get_balance: REAL
        do Result := balance end
feature -- Operations
    deposit (amount: REAL)
        require amount > 0
        do balance := balance + amount end
    withdraw (amount: REAL)
        require
            amount > 0
            amount <= balance
        do balance := balance - amount end
end

content.title: Analyze & Extend: Overdraft Protection
content.instructions: 1) Analyze: Why is balance private while account_number is public? What quality attributes does this support? 2) Apply: Sketch how to add overdraft_limit feature and modify withdraw to allow overdrafts up to the limit. Which feature clause? What precondition changes? 3) Share one design decision with a neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: Walk through encapsulation: balance is feature {NONE} (private), enforcing information hiding. Public interface: get_balance (query), deposit/withdraw (commands). Highlight require clauses as Design by Contract preview—preconditions enforce correctness. Launch activity: students first analyze design rationale (why this encapsulation?), then apply by extending functionality. This combines analytical thinking with practical application. During debrief, emphasize that overdraft_limit should be private, withdraw precondition becomes 'amount <= balance + overdraft_limit', supporting extendibility without breaking encapsulation. Collect solutions showing different approaches to initialization and validation.

slides.title: Course Roadmap: Your Learning Path

content.prompt: Course dependency graph showing progression of topics. Foundation layer: 'Classes & Objects', 'Encapsulation'. Construction layer (arrows from foundation): 'Inheritance', 'Polymorphism', 'Genericity'. Architecture layer (arrows from construction): 'Design Patterns', 'Large-Scale Structure'. Engineering layer (arrows from all): 'Agile Methods', 'Requirements', 'Quality Processes'. Use different colors for each layer, arrows showing dependencies.

content.title: Map Your Learning: Predict & Connect
content.instructions: Study the roadmap. Choose ONE upcoming topic (inheritance, polymorphism, design patterns, or agile methods). In 3 minutes: 1) Predict: Which quality attribute(s) will this topic primarily support? Why? 2) Connect: How might this topic build on encapsulation from today? Write 2-3 sentences, then share with a neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: Present the roadmap as a learning journey with clear dependencies. Launch activity to activate predictive thinking: students analyze how future topics connect to today's foundations and quality attributes. Common predictions: inheritance supports extendibility/reusability, polymorphism enables robustness through flexible interfaces, design patterns support reusability, agile supports correctness through iteration. During debrief, validate predictions and emphasize that each layer builds systematically—you can't master patterns without polymorphism, can't apply agile without understanding quality attributes. This metacognitive exercise helps students see the course as integrated rather than isolated topics.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

items: Four quality attributes: correctness, robustness, extendibility, reusability
Object-oriented programming supports quality through encapsulation
Classes are templates, objects are instances
Eiffel provides clear notation for learning OO concepts

(4) Classes and objects are fundamental concepts, with encapsulation as key principle. (5) Eiffel notation will be our vehicle for learning. Remind students of action items: install Eiffel, read assigned chapters, attend tutorials. Preview next lecture: inheritance (extending classes) and polymorphism (flexibility through type relationships). Encourage questions and office hour visits.
